# Theorem
There are infinitely many primes of the form $4k+3$.

## Proof
We argue by contradiction. Suppose there are only finitely many primes congruent to $3 \pmod 4$. Call them $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$. This list is nonempty, since $3$ is such a prime.

Define
$$N = 4p_1p_2\cdots p_n - 1.$$

We record three facts about $N$.

1. **$N > 1$.** Since $p_1p_2\cdots p_n \ge 3$, we have $N \ge 4\cdot 3 - 1 = 11$.
2. **$N \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.** We have $N = 4(p_1\cdots p_n - 1) + 3$.
3. **$N$ is odd.** This follows from fact 2. Hence $2 \nmid N$.

**Key lemma.** Every odd prime is congruent to $1$ or $3 \pmod 4$. If $a \equiv 1$ and $b \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, then $ab \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. By induction, any product of integers that are each $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$ is itself $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$.

**Applying the lemma.** Since $N > 1$, it factors as a product of primes. All of these primes are odd, since $N$ is odd. If every one of them were $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, the lemma would give $N \equiv 1 \pmod 4$. This contradicts $N \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Therefore $N$ has at least one prime divisor $q$ with $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$.

**The contradiction.** By our assumption, $q$ must be one of the primes $p_i$ on the list. Then $q$ divides $4p_1p_2\cdots p_n$, and $q$ also divides $N$. Hence $q$ divides their difference:
$$4p_1p_2\cdots p_n - N = 1.$$
But no prime divides $1$. This is a contradiction.

**Conclusion.** The assumption that there are only finitely many primes of the form $4k+3$ is false. Hence there are infinitely many such primes. $\blacksquare$
